unit.title: Perform gas tungsten arc welding process to AWS specification.(Plate)

summary: This unit is about gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW, or TIG) of plate to an AWS specification. You will learn to work to a qualified procedure (WPS), understand what a welder's qualification covers, set up the machine, tungsten, gas and filler for carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium, and weld groove and fillet test coupons in all positions. You will also learn to inspect and test them, find the cause of each defect, and run a fair, well-recorded qualification test.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It takes the TIG welding you learned on sheet in the flat and horizontal positions and applies it to **plate welded to the AWS code the Centre uses**: groove welds (butt welds) and fillet welds in all positions, welded to a **welding procedure specification (WPS)**, then inspected, bend tested, broken or etched, and recorded.

GTAW gives the cleanest, most controlled welds of the common processes. There is no flux and no slag, and the welder controls the heat and the filler separately. That control is why GTAW is used for roots, thin and critical work, stainless steel and aluminium. It is also why GTAW is unforgiving: dirt, draughts and poor technique show at once.

**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees who can already TIG weld sheet in the flat and horizontal positions, and who will now weld plate in all positions to a procedure, take and help run qualification tests, and lead others.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work to the specification and WPS
Find a qualified WPS for the job, follow every variable, and record what was used.
Check a welder's WPQ for positions, thickness, backing, filler and continuity before giving out work.
Control UV, fume, argon, electrical and high-frequency hazards, tungsten grinding dust, solvents and etching acids.
Choose current and polarity, tungsten, cup, gas flow and the machine's start, slope and post-flow settings.
Choose the filler for the metal, and clean, fit up and tack plate to the standard GTAW needs.
Weld groove coupons in 1G to 4G, open root or on backing, and fillets in 1F to 4F.
Inspect by eye; prepare and judge bend, fillet break and macro etch tests; link each failure to its cause.
Run a test and keep records
Plan and witness a fair test, record real values, work out heat input and quantities, and complete WPQs.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the specification and WPS, welder qualification, preparation, filler metal, arc starting, set-up, tungsten, technique, positions, safety, testing, defects, records, shielding gas and calculations.
A **written paper** with short answers and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practicals**: open-root single-V groove coupons in carbon steel plate in 3G and 4G with bend tests and draft WPQs; and 3F and 4F fillet welds with fillet break and macro etch tests and a PQR-style record.

blocks.note: In a qualification test the coupon must be welded exactly as the WPS says, in the position set, and without being moved. Practise that way from the start.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Document
What it is
rows: The written method: base metal and thickness range, joint design, filler class and size, tungsten type and size, current and polarity, gas and flow rate, position, passes, preheat
The record of a test plate welded to a draft WPS: the **real values** used (current, voltage, travel speed, gas flow, passes) and the test results
A welder's record: the process, positions, thickness range, backing, filler group and results of the welder's test

blocks.p: A WPS tells you **how to weld**; a WPQ shows that a **welder passed**. Under many codes, a GTAW procedure is not "prequalified": before it is used on a job, a test plate must be welded to it, tested and recorded on a PQR. Follow the code the Centre uses.

flow: Write a draft WPS for the plate, joint, position, filler, tungsten, current, gas and passes
A skilled welder welds a test plate to the draft; a witness records the real values
The plate is inspected by eye, then cut and tested as the code asks (bend tests, and sometimes tensile tests and a macro etch)
The real values and results go on a signed PQR
If it passes, the WPS is finalised from the PQR within the ranges the code allows; if it fails, the cause is found, the draft changed and a new plate tested

blocks.p: Some WPS details are **essential variables**: changing one needs a new procedure test. For GTAW, under many codes, these include the base metal group, the filler classification, the type of shielding gas, the current type and polarity, and the thickness range. So a WPS qualified on DCEN does not cover welding on AC, and a WPS qualified with pure argon does not cover another gas, until a WPS that covers them is approved.
A PQR records current, voltage and travel speed because together they give the **heat input** (arc energy), which affects the strength and toughness of the weld. Some codes limit it.

blocks.note: **Arc energy (kJ/mm) = volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1 000).** Example: 11 V, 110 A, 100 mm/min: 11 × 110 × 60 = 72 600; 100 × 1 000 = 100 000; 72 600 ÷ 100 000 = **0.73 kJ/mm**. Some codes then multiply by an efficiency factor for the process; use the method your code gives.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Plate test
Groove positions covered
Fillet positions covered
rows: None (fillet tests do not cover grooves)

ul: **Backing:** a groove test on a backing strip generally covers only joints with backing. An open-root test covers both open-root and backed joints.
**Thickness:** a test plate covers only a range of thickness from the code's table. Check the job thickness is inside it.
**Filler:** the test covers the filler group used.
**Pipe:** a plate test covers pipe only above a size set by the code.
**Continuity:** the qualification stays in force only while the welder keeps using GTAW, often with no gap longer than six months.

blocks.note: Check the code's own tables before giving out work: they decide what a test covers, and they differ between codes and editions.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Hazard
Why it matters in GTAW
Controls
rows: The GTAW arc gives very strong UV. Bright aluminium and stainless plate reflect it, burning the neck, arms and the skin under the chin
All skin covered: collar done up, no gaps at the wrists
UV turns oxygen in the air round the arc into ozone, which irritates the lungs; worst with aluminium and high currents
Light compared with MMAW, but stainless steel fume contains chromium and nickel compounds
Heavier than air; collects in pits, tanks and low closed spaces and pushes out the air, without warning
Never weld or purge in a closed space without a permit and gas testing
Cylinders chained upright; closed after use
Live torch and cables; HF starting sends a high-voltage spark that can upset computers, phones and card machines nearby
Check cables, torch and foot pedal; keep them dry, on a dry mat or board if the floor is damp
Keep electronic equipment away from HF sets
People with pacemakers or other medical implants keep away from HF and the arc unless their doctor says it is safe
Grinding dust in the lungs; **thoriated** tungsten (red tip) is slightly radioactive
Use the dedicated, guarded tungsten grinder with extraction
Prefer non-thoriated tungstens where the WPS allows
Acetone burns easily. **Chlorinated** solvents (some degreasers and brake cleaners) turn into poisonous phosgene gas in UV light
Let acetone dry fully and keep rags and cans away from the arc
Never use chlorinated solvents in or near a welding bay
Burns to skin and eyes; fumes
Always add **acid to water**, slowly, never water to acid
Plate looks the same hot or cold

blocks.note: Gas welding shades (about 4–6) are far too light for any electric arc. If the pool is hard to see at the right shade, improve the light on the work and keep the lens clean; do not drop to a lighter shade.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Current
Heat
Used for
rows: About two-thirds of the heat goes into the work; the tungsten stays cool
Carbon steel, stainless steel, copper and most metals
Heat shared; the electrode-positive half of each cycle breaks up the oxide skin (**cleaning action**)
Most heat goes into the tungsten, which overheats

blocks.p: Aluminium's oxide skin melts at about 2 050 °C, far above the metal's 660 °C. On AC, the electrode-positive half cycles blast the oxide off so the pool can fuse, while the electrode-negative half cycles give penetration and keep the tungsten cool.

head: Setting
What it does
Typical guide
rows: **HF** (high frequency) or **lift-arc** starts the arc without the tungsten scratching the plate
Scratch starting is banned on most test plates, as it can leave tungsten in the weld
Gas flows before the arc, purging air from the torch and the joint
About half a second or more
Raises the current gently at the start
A second or two, or as the WPS says
Lowers the current slowly at the end so the crater fills and does not crack
Gas keeps flowing after the arc stops, to shield the hot tungsten and the crater
Often about 1 second for every 10 A, so about 10–12 seconds at 110 A
Switches between a peak and a background current; the pool cools a little in each background period
Helps control the pool in vertical and overhead work and on thin plate

blocks.note: If the tungsten comes out blue, purple or black after each stop, or the crater is dark and oxidised, the post-flow is too short. A bright, silver tungsten and a shiny crater show the post-flow is doing its job.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Cups** (nozzles) are sized in sixteenths of an inch: a No. 6 cup is about 9.5 mm across, a No. 8 about 12.7 mm. A bigger cup gives a wider gas cover.

A **gas lens** (a fine mesh screen in the collet body) makes the gas flow smooth and even, so the tungsten can stick out further, often about 10 mm or more, to reach into a groove root or a corner, with good cover.
**Stick-out** with a standard collet body is usually about 3–6 mm; further than that, the gas cover is poor.
**Shielding gas** for carbon steel, stainless and aluminium is usually pure **argon**. Argon-helium mixes give more heat on thick aluminium and copper.
Never use argon mixed with CO2 or oxygen (MIG mixes) for GTAW: they attack and burn away the tungsten.

Set the **flow** on the flowmeter, usually about 7–12 litres a minute for plate with a No. 6–8 cup (a little more with a gas lens). **Too much** flow is as bad as too little: the gas comes out turbulent and drags air into the shield.
Stainless steel open roots need **back purging**: argon fed behind the joint, or the back of the root oxidises into a rough, dark crust ("sugaring").

blocks.p: A leak in the gas hose, a loose torch fitting, a missing O-ring or a cracked cup can draw air into the gas stream even when the flowmeter reads correctly. If porosity suddenly appears after a torch part has been changed, check every connection between the flowmeter and the cup.

head: Type (AWS)
Tip colour (AWS)
Use and points to know
rows: AC for aluminium; forms a balled end. On DCEN it erodes and the arc wanders: not for steel
Good DC starts at low current; also used on AC
Good on DC and AC; a common all-round choice
Long the usual DC tungsten; **slightly radioactive**: grind only on a dedicated grinder with extraction

blocks.note: Colour codes differ between the AWS and ISO systems for some types. Read the packet as well as the tip colour, and use the type the WPS names.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Diameter
Typical current range
rows: Up to about 250 A; a common all-round size for plate

blocks.p: Too small a tungsten for the current melts at the tip and can drop tungsten into the weld. Too big a tungsten at low current gives an unsteady, wandering arc and poor starts.

ul: Grind on a **dedicated** wheel, so the tungsten does not pick up other metals.
Grind with the marks running **along** the tungsten, not round it. Lengthways marks give a steady arc that stays on the point; circular marks make it wander.
Make the ground point about 2 to 2½ times the diameter long, and leave a tiny flat on the tip for higher currents, so the point does not melt off.
If the tungsten touches the pool or the rod, **stop**: break off or grind away the contaminated end, regrind the point, and grind out the contaminated spot in the weld before going on.

sections.title: Filler metals and preparing the plate

head: Filler
Use
Why
rows: Contains several deoxidisers (aluminium, titanium and zirconium, as well as silicon and manganese), so the weld metal is sound even with traces of oxide
High silicon and manganese; also common, especially for MIG
Matches the alloy; low carbon resists corrosion at the weld
Contains molybdenum, like the plate, for corrosion resistance
Extra alloy allows for dilution by the carbon steel, so the weld stays stainless and crack-resistant
Aluminium-magnesium alloys and where more strength is needed

ul: GTAW rods are usually about 900 mm to 1 m long, stamped or flagged with their class at one end so classes are never mixed up.
Common sizes: 1.6 mm, 2.4 mm and 3.2 mm. Use the size on the WPS.
Keep rods in their sealed, labelled tubes; handle with clean gloves. Rods left dusty or oily are wiped with solvent and dried, or replaced with clean ones. Snip off a rod end that has oxidised.

blocks.p: Anything on the joint, such as oil, paint, mill scale, rust, oxide or marker, goes into the pool and causes **porosity**, **lack of fusion** and an unsteady arc, and can contaminate the tungsten. GTAW has no flux to deal with it, so the joint must be cleaner than for MMAW.

head: Metal
Preparation
rows: Grind the bevels and about 25 mm of both faces to bright metal; wipe with solvent and let it dry
Use only stainless-steel brushes and discs kept for stainless, so no carbon steel is picked up (it rusts later); wipe with solvent
Degrease with solvent first, then brush off the oxide with a stainless brush kept only for aluminium; weld soon after, as the oxide grows back

head: Joint
Typical preparation (follow the WPS)
rows: 60–75° included angle, root face about 0–1.5 mm, root gap about 2–3 mm
A wider gap onto a steel backing strip, as the WPS shows; the strip must sit **tight** against both plates
Upright plate fitted tight to the base plate, with small tacks at the ends

flow: Check the plates are the grade and thickness on the WPS; mark them with the test number
Bevel, then grind and clean to bright metal on both faces; set the root face and check the angle with a bevel protractor
Wipe with solvent and let it dry fully
Lay the plates flat, set the root gap with a spacer, and check there is no step between them; on a backed joint, clamp the backing strip tight
Tack each end with small, fully fused tacks, and feather (taper) their ends
Re-check the gap; fix the coupon in the stand in the test position, at a comfortable height
Once fixed, the coupon stays in position until the test is finished

blocks.note: A gap between a backing strip and the plates lets air and contamination in under the root, giving porosity and lack of fusion along the strip. Clamp the strip tight before tacking it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Arc length:** about the tungsten diameter or a little less. A long arc gives a wide, shallow, poorly shielded weld; a very short one risks touching the pool.
**Torch angle:** square to the joint from the side (or halving the angle between the plates on a fillet), tipped about 10–20° so the tungsten points the way you are travelling.
**Filler:** held low, about 15–20° to the plate, fed into the **leading edge** of the pool. Keep the hot end inside the gas shield between dips.
**Never let the tungsten touch the pool or the rod.**
Start in the joint (or on a run-on tab), never on the plate surface beside it. A stray arc strike leaves a hard spot or a small crack.
Finish with the **downslope** or the foot pedal, adding a last dab of rod to fill the crater, and hold the torch over it through the post-flow.

head: Method
How it works
Used for
rows: Rod dipped into the front of the pool, then withdrawn, in rhythm with the torch moving forward
The rod is laid in the root and melted in as the torch moves along it
Roots, especially with a tight gap
The rod is fed steadily into the pool by the fingers
The cup rests on the bevel faces and is rocked from side to side as the torch moves forward, so the arc length and travel stay very steady
Roots and fill passes in grooves, especially on pipe and thick plate

blocks.p: On an open root, keep a small **keyhole** at the front of the pool: a hole that shows both root faces are melting through. If the keyhole closes up, the root is not penetrating: slow down a little and hold the arc at the front of the pool until it reopens, and check the gap ahead. If it grows, speed up or reduce the heat. Add rod steadily so the root bead is even inside.

ul: Clean each run with a stainless wire brush or a grinder before the next. ER70S-2 and other deoxidised fillers leave small, brown, glassy **silicon islands** on the surface; brush or grind them off, or they cause inclusions and poor fusion under the next run.
Pause at each side of a weave so the toes fill; cross the middle a little faster, or the bead peaks in the middle with undercut at both toes.
Lay the cap slightly past the bevel edges, even in width, with the height within the code's limit.

head: Position
Technique
Faults to watch
rows: Too much penetration with a wide gap
Torch nearly square to the plate, tipped slightly up; rod fed at the **upper** edge of the pool
Sag and overlap onto the lower plate; undercut on the upper
Torch pointing up at a small angle; rod into the top of the pool; build on the shelf of metal below; pause at the sides
Undercut at the toes; peaked bead; sagging pool
Small pool: lower current (pulse helps), short arc, small dabs of rod
Pool dropping; concave root; lack of fusion at the toes
Torch halving the angle, pointing up; rod at the top of the pool; pause at each toe; equal legs
Undercut on the upright; uneven legs
Small pool; short arc; rod fed at the upper (overhead) plate
Sagging; unequal legs; lack of root fusion

blocks.note: Stand or sit so you can move your whole arm smoothly along the joint, and brace your hand. Most out-of-position faults come from a welder who cannot see the pool or is straining to reach.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Defect
Main causes
Prevention
rows: Tungsten touching the pool or rod; scratch starting; current too high for the tungsten; cracked tip
HF or lift-arc start; right tungsten size; steady arc; stop and regrind after a dip
Too little or too much gas flow; draughts; leaks in the gas line; dirty plate or rod
Correct flow; screens; leak-free torch; clean metal
Lack of fusion (side wall or root)
Too little heat; travel too fast; arc aimed off one side
Correct current; aim and pause at both sides; melt each edge before adding rod
Gap too small; root face too thick; keyhole lost
Fit up to the WPS; keep a keyhole
Overhead pool pulled back; too much heat
Small pool; correct heat; enough rod at the root
Gap too wide; too much heat; too slow
Too much heat; no pause at the toes; arc too long
Pause at the toes; correct heat; short arc
Pool sagging over the lower plate (2G); too much rod; too slow
Rod at the upper edge; correct speed
Downslope and a last dab of rod
Striking outside the joint; torch touching the plate
Start in the joint or on a tab; keep the torch and cables tidy
Purge behind the root with argon
Control the fill; the code limits reinforcement because a high cap leaves a sharp notch at the toes

blocks.p: Every coupon is inspected by eye first, on both sides, in good light. Typical limits (from the code the Centre uses): no cracks; complete fusion; undercut no deeper than about 1 mm; cap and root reinforcement within about 3 mm; no arc strikes; craters filled. A coupon that fails visual inspection is not bend tested.

flow: Remove any backing strip flush, by machining or grinding
Cut off and discard the ends of the coupon, where the starts and stops are not typical, as the code's drawing shows
Mark out the strips (often about 38 mm wide) from the places the code sets, and label each one
Cut by saw or machine, not by torch near the weld
Grind the cap and root flush, with the grinding marks running **along** the strip, and round the long edges slightly
Bend in a guided bend jig with the former (plunger) size the code sets for that thickness: a smaller former stretches the strip more than the test allows
Examine the outside of the bend and measure any open defects

head: Strip
In tension (outside of the bend)
A failure usually shows
rows: Lack of fusion in the cap or fill at the side walls (often from fast travel or too little heat at the edges); open pores
Lack of root fusion or penetration (gap too small, root face too thick, too little current); a tungsten inclusion can start a crack
Faults through the thickness; used on thicker plate

blocks.p: Many codes reject an open defect longer than about 3 mm on the outside of a bend. Where the code allows, radiography may be used instead of bend tests for a welder's groove test.

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: The upright plate is bent over (with the root of the weld in tension) until the weld breaks
Whether the root is fused into both plates, and any porosity or inclusions inside
A slice is cut across the weld, ground smooth, polished with fine abrasive and etched with a suitable acid solution under supervision
Root fusion, penetration into both plates, leg sizes and the shape inside

blocks.note: A macro etch shows what no surface check can: whether the weld really fused into both plates and the root. If one plate shows an unfused line along its face, the arc was aimed too much at the other plate, or the torch moved on before that side melted.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Running a test, records and calculations

blocks.h: Planning and running a fair test

flow: Check the WPS; gather plates of the right grade and thickness, filler, tungstens and argon; check every set, flowmeter, torch and stand
Mark each coupon with a number and the welder's name, so coupons cannot be swapped
Brief the trainees on the WPS, the test rules and safety
Witness the fit-up; check each coupon is fixed in its stated position and stays there
Watch the welding and record the real settings; note anything outside the WPS; do not help
Each trainee welds only his or her own coupon, all of it
Inspect each coupon by eye and record the result before any are cut
Cut, label and bend strips from the set places in front of a witness
Record every result, pass or fail, on the WPQ forms; keep the strips until the records are signed
Go over each failed strip with the trainee and plan practice for the retest the code allows

ul: Welder, coupon number, date, WPS number and revision.
Base metal, thickness, position, and backing or open root.
Filler class and size; tungsten type and size; cup size.
Current, polarity, voltage, gas type and flow; travel speed or run times; number of passes.
Any stops, repairs or events during the test.

head: Sum
Example
rows: Torches × litres a minute × minutes. 4 torches × 10 L/min × 120 min = **4 800 litres**
Contents ÷ flow. 9 000 litres ÷ 10 L/min = 900 minutes = **15 hours** of gas flow
Length ÷ time. 250 mm in 5 minutes = **50 mm/min**
Coupons × strips each. 4 trainees × 2 coupons × 2 strips = **16 strips**
Strip width plus one saw cut each; round down. 160 mm of good weld, 38 mm strips, 3 mm cuts: 160 ÷ 41 = 3.9, so **3 strips**

blocks.note: Post-flow and purging use gas as well as the arc, so allow extra argon. Check sums twice, and round strips and cylinders the safe way: down for strips you can cut, up for cylinders you must order.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the WPS, PQR and WPQ, and how a GTAW procedure is qualified.
I can name typical GTAW essential variables and work out arc energy from volts, amps and travel speed.
I can say which positions, joints and thicknesses a plate test generally covers, including backing and continuity.
I can control the hazards of GTAW: UV, ozone, fume, argon, HF, thoriated tungsten, solvents and acids.
I can choose the current and polarity for steel, stainless steel and aluminium.
I can set pre-flow, slopes, post-flow and pulse, and choose a cup, gas lens and gas flow.
I can choose, size and grind a tungsten for the job.
I can choose the filler for carbon steel, stainless steel, dissimilar joints and aluminium.
I can clean, fit up and tack plate coupons, open root or on backing.
I can weld groove coupons in 1G to 4G and fillets in 1F to 4F, with a keyhole root and clean runs.
I can name GTAW defects, their causes and their prevention.
I can prepare, bend and judge face, root and side bends, and carry out fillet break and macro etch tests safely.
I can plan and witness a fair test and complete the records and calculations.

terms: The oxide-removing effect of the electrode-positive half of each AC cycle
Argon fed behind a root to stop it oxidising
The ceramic nozzle that directs the shielding gas
Direct current electrode negative: the usual GTAW polarity for steel
Lowering the current slowly at the end of a run to fill the crater
Breaking a fillet weld open with its root in tension to see the fusion
A fine screen in the torch that smooths the gas flow
Starting the arc with a high-frequency spark, without touching the tungsten to the work
The small hole at the front of a root pool showing full penetration
Laying the rod in the root and melting it in as the torch moves
A polished, etched slice showing the weld's fusion and shape
Gas flowing after the arc stops, to shield the tungsten and crater
Small glassy deposits left on GTAW and MIG runs by deoxidisers
How far the tungsten extends beyond the cup
A piece of tungsten trapped in the weld
Rocking the cup on the bevel faces to move the torch steadily along

c1.title: Setting up GTAW bays in Half Way Tree
c1.text: Before a GTAW plate session at a training centre in Half Way Tree, St Andrew, Monique is checking four bays for carbon steel work on DCEN at about 120 A. The only new tungstens in the store are green-tipped. Some red-tipped tungstens are also in a drawer. One flowmeter is set at 25 litres a minute with a No. 6 cup.

c2.title: A stainless counter for a hotel kitchen in Treasure Beach
c2.text: A shop is making a 316L stainless steel counter for a hotel kitchen in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth, with an aluminium splash plate on one side. A helper has brought a spray can of brake cleaner to degrease the stainless before welding.

c3.title: 3G and 4G coupons in Frankfield
c3.text: At a centre in Frankfield, Clarendon, trainees are welding open-root single-V coupons in 10 mm carbon steel plate in the 3G and 4G positions with ER70S-2 rod and 2.4 mm tungstens. During Dwight's 3G root the keyhole keeps closing up. After each fill run, small brown glassy spots are left on the weld. Tashana cannot reach the root with her standard collet body unless the tungsten sticks well out of the cup. Another trainee wants to take his 4G coupon down to the bench to grind the root.

c4.title: A fillet procedure test in Lionel Town
c4.text: A shop in Lionel Town, Clarendon, is proving a GTAW fillet procedure on 6 mm carbon steel plate in the 3F position. The witness records 12 V, 120 A and a travel speed of 80 mm a minute. On one macro etch, the weld has fused well into the upright plate, but a thin unfused line runs along the face of the base plate. The welder, Rajay, already holds a 3G groove qualification on the same plate.

c5.title: Porosity in the bays in Port Maria
c5.text: At a shop in Port Maria, St Mary, porosity suddenly appears in one welder's carbon steel welds after the torch hose has been changed. The flowmeter still reads 10 litres a minute, the plate is clean and the bay is screened. The full argon cylinder for that bay holds about 9 000 litres.

questions.q: Can the green-tipped tungstens be used for the carbon steel work on DCEN?
o: Yes, all tungstens work the same on every current
No: pure tungsten is for AC; use ceriated or lanthanated
Yes, if the current is raised so the tip balls
No: green tungstens may be used only for stainless steel
questions.why: Green is pure tungsten, made for AC on aluminium. On DCEN it erodes and the arc wanders. Ceriated or lanthanated tungstens (or another type the WPS names) give steady DC arcs.

questions.q: If the red-tipped tungstens are used, what must be done when they are ground?
o: Only on a dedicated grinder with dust extraction
Grind them with the marks running round the tip
Grind them on the bench grinder used for drill bits
Wet them first so they do not overheat on the wheel
questions.why: Red is 2% thoriated tungsten, which is slightly radioactive; its dust must not be breathed. It is ground only on a dedicated, guarded grinder with extraction, and many centres choose non-thoriated types instead.

questions.q: What is likely to happen with the flowmeter set at 25 litres a minute on a No. 6 cup?
o: The weld will be extra clean, because more gas means better cover
The tungsten will run too cold and the arc will not start
The flow is turbulent and drags air in, causing porosity
The argon will cool the pool so much that it will not fuse
questions.why: Too much gas comes out of a small cup turbulent and pulls air into the shield. Usual flows for plate with a No. 6–8 cup are about 7–12 litres a minute.

questions.q: Which filter shade suits this work at about 120 A?
o: About 5, as for gas welding
About 3, so the pool is easy to see
Clear glasses, as GTAW gives no spatter
About 12, from the shade chart
questions.why: Shade charts give about 11–12 for GTAW at 50–150 A. Gas welding shades are far too light for an arc, and the strong UV of GTAW burns unprotected eyes quickly.

questions.q: Which filler rod should be used on the 316L counter?
o: ER308L
ER316L
ER70S-2
questions.why: ER316L matches 316L stainless, including its molybdenum, for the same corrosion resistance. ER308L suits 304, ER70S-2 is for carbon steel and ER4043 for aluminium.

questions.q: Why must the brake cleaner not be used near the welding bay?
o: It leaves an oily film that stops the argon flowing
It rusts stainless steel within a few days
Its vapour turns into phosgene gas in UV light
It makes the tungsten tip melt into a round ball
questions.why: Many brake cleaners and degreasers are chlorinated. The arc's UV turns their vapour into phosgene, a poisonous gas. Use a non-chlorinated solvent such as acetone, let it dry fully, and keep rags and cans away from the arc.

questions.q: Why is the aluminium splash plate welded on AC rather than DCEN?
o: Its electrode-positive half cycles break up the oxide
AC puts more heat into the tungsten to melt the aluminium
AC needs no argon, so the plate is not contaminated
Aluminium cannot carry direct current at all
questions.why: Aluminium's oxide melts far above the metal. On AC, each electrode-positive half cycle blasts the oxide off (the cleaning action), while the electrode-negative half gives penetration.

questions.q: What should Dwight do when the keyhole closes up during his root?
o: Speed up so the pool does not get too hot and sag
Lengthen the arc so the heat spreads right across the gap
Add more rod so the root fills up from the face side
Slow down and hold the arc at the front until it reopens
questions.why: A closed keyhole means the root faces are no longer melting through. Holding the arc at the leading edge a little longer brings it back. Check the gap ahead too: a tight gap closes the keyhole.

questions.q: What should be done about the small brown glassy spots after each fill run?
o: Brush or grind them off before the next run
Leave them: the next run will melt and float them away
Weld the next run at a lower current to avoid them
Change to a filler with no deoxidisers in it
questions.why: The spots are silicon islands from the deoxidisers in ER70S-2. They are glassy, so they do not melt in easily and can cause inclusions and lack of fusion under the next run. Clean every run before the next.

questions.q: How can Tashana get a long stick-out to reach the root and still keep good gas cover?
o: Raise the flow to 25 litres a minute with the standard collet body
Fit a gas lens, which gives a smooth, even gas flow
Change to a much smaller cup so the gas comes out faster
Grind a longer point on the tungsten instead
questions.why: A gas lens smooths the gas into an even column, so the tungsten can stick out about 10 mm or more with good cover. Extra flow through a standard collet body just makes the gas turbulent.

questions.q: What should the assessor tell the trainee who wants to take his 4G coupon down to grind the root?
o: Allow it, as long as he refits it at the same height afterwards
Allow it for the root only, as it is the hardest part
Refuse: it stays fixed in position; he may grind it where it is
Allow it, but take a mark off his final result
questions.why: The position is part of what is tested. Taking the coupon down and refitting it means part of the work was not done in the 4G position. Cleaning and grinding are done with the coupon fixed in the stand.

questions.q: What is the arc energy for this weld?
o: About 1.08 kJ/mm
About 0.11 kJ/mm
About 18 kJ/mm
About 0.48 kJ/mm
questions.why: 12 × 120 × 60 = 86 400, and 80 × 1 000 = 80 000; 86 400 ÷ 80 000 = 1.08 kJ/mm. Volts × amps gives joules a second; × 60 gives joules a minute; dividing by mm a minute gives joules per mm, and ÷ 1 000 turns joules into kilojoules.

questions.q: What most likely caused the unfused line along the base plate in the macro etch?
o: The argon flow was set too low for a fillet weld
The arc was aimed mostly at the upright plate
The plates were cleaned too well before welding
The tungsten was ground with the marks running along it
questions.why: A fillet must fuse into both plates. An unfused line on one plate's face shows the heat went mainly into the other plate. Aim the torch to halve the angle, and make sure the base plate melts before adding rod.

questions.q: Generally, does Rajay's 3G groove qualification cover him for 3F fillets on this plate?
o: No: fillet welds always need their own separate test
No: a groove test covers only the flat fillet position
Only if the fillets are smaller than 3 mm
Yes: a groove test generally covers fillets too
questions.why: Under many codes a groove test covers fillet welds in the positions it qualifies, within the code's limits. A fillet test, though, does not cover groove welds. Check the code's table.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the sudden porosity?
o: Air drawn in at a leaking hose or torch connection
The flowmeter reading 10 litres a minute is too low
The plate was cleaned with acetone before welding
The cylinder is too full, so the gas comes out too cold
questions.why: A loose fitting, a missing O-ring or a damaged new hose can pull air into the gas stream even when the flowmeter reads correctly. Leak-test every connection from the flowmeter to the cup.

questions.q: At 10 litres a minute, about how many hours of gas flow will the 9 000-litre cylinder give?
o: 90 hours
1.5 hours
15 hours
9 hours
questions.why: 9 000 ÷ 10 = 900 minutes, and 900 ÷ 60 = 15 hours. Pre-flow, post-flow and purging also use gas, so the real arc time will be less.

questions.q: A new trainee tells the instructor he has a heart pacemaker. What is the safe advice about the GTAW bay?
o: He may weld, as long as he uses lift-arc start
He may weld, if he wears a thicker leather jacket
He may weld at low currents, below about 50 A
He stays away until his doctor says it is safe
questions.why: High-frequency starting and the magnetic fields round welding cables can upset pacemakers and other implants. He should keep away until his doctor gives clear advice, and the Centre should follow it.

questions.q: What is "walking the cup"?
o: Rocking the cup on the bevel faces to move the torch along
Moving the gas cylinder along with the welder on its trolley
Changing to a bigger cup at each new pass
Lifting the cup off the plate between dabs of rod
questions.why: In walking the cup, the cup rests on the bevel faces and is rocked from side to side as it moves forward. It keeps the arc length and travel very steady, especially on roots and fill passes.

questions.q: After each stop, a welder's tungsten comes out blue-black and the crater looks dark. Which setting should be changed?
o: Pre-flow: it should be made shorter
Post-flow: it should be made longer
Upslope: it should be made faster
Pulse: it should be switched off
questions.why: A discoloured tungsten and an oxidised crater show they were not shielded while still hot. Lengthen the post-flow (often about 1 second per 10 A) and hold the torch over the crater until it stops.

questions.q: A trainee tacks a 1G coupon onto its backing strip, but there is a visible gap between the strip and one plate. What should be done?
o: Weld it as it is, as the root will fill the gap
Run the root at a higher current to melt the gap closed
Clamp the strip tight to both plates and re-tack it
Grind the backing strip off and weld it as an open root
questions.why: A gap under the backing lets air and dirt in under the root and leaves an unfused line along the strip. The strip is clamped tight to both plates before it is tacked. Removing it would also change the joint from the one the WPS gives.
